summary:
Same-sex conduct between men was decriminalised in Barbados in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program. The Human Dignity Trust places the Barbados case within a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes across the Eastern Caribbean, and a High Court ruling on sodomy published in May 2023 found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is recent and specific. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward, suffering serious injuries including to her throat. He was convicted in April 2019 and sentenced to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or serve three months in prison, with no jail time handed down. Hoffmann has written first-person about the visibility and danger trans people face on the island.

Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category, and the state has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration. In 2011 the government said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada. In 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean said such applications risked abusing the Canadian refugee system, noting that two of nine Canadian applications had been denied, and a Guyanese newspaper that year reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States. On the entry side, the 'Welcome Stamp' remote-work visa introduced in July 2020 initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse before being changed to permit same-sex spouses.

Employment is the sharpest practical exposure for a trans visitor working locally. The Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars employment discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status. Hoffmann argues the Act excludes trans workers because gender identity and gender expression are not listed as protected grounds; reporting from August 2020 describes trans Barbadians being fired or denied jobs for 'dressing wrong'.

No same-sex relationship or union is recognised. The government ruled out same-sex marriage in June 2016, and in September 2020 announced only a plan to recognise 'some form' of civil union followed by a referendum on gay marriage; critics called the civil union proposal 'unnecessarily vague' and expected the referendum to fail, and neither had been enacted as of the source account. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging sections 9 and 12 of the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154), and the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019; failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility has been stated plainly and repeatedly. In 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite said Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and after UK Prime Minister David Cameron's 2011 CHOGM warning linking aid to sodomy laws he said Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a 'cheap political trick' because its report did not mention same-sex marriage.

Religious and media pressure runs alongside that official line. Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued that discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and human rights activists report that American evangelical ministers arriving in Barbados have spread homophobic rhetoric more widely. The Barbados Nation newspaper's informal comment line drew opposition to a proposed gay tourism package. Set against this, the Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church oppose the buggery law while respecting LGBT rights, and Prime Minister Mia Mottley, elected in May 2018, is reported as pro-LGBT.

The constitutional litigation is part of a regional pattern rather than a Barbadian exception: the Human Dignity Trust documents equivalent challenges across the Eastern Caribbean, and the Inter-American petition on the Sexual Offences Act remains an open regional channel for a binding outcome.

Community visibility exists despite the risk. The Trans Day of Remembrance vigil held in Barbados in November 2018 was the second of its kind, organised with the National Organisation of Women, a local ally and veteran trans advocates. Barbados Gays, Lesbians and All-Sexuals Against Discrimination (BGLAD), founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed, was set up to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue, and Pride events have served an awareness-raising function, from a small first event in November 2017 to a parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown, in July 2018.
localsOnly:
Family formation is restricted for resident same-sex couples. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by statute, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families. The only parenting-related service identified is the Barbados Fertility Centre, which offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.

The 2020 employment statute is the principal domestic protection, but its coverage of trans workers is contested. Parliament passed the Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act in August 2020 with sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status as protected grounds; Hoffmann's position is that the omission of gender identity and gender expression leaves trans employees outside it, consistent with reports of trans Barbadians being dismissed or refused work for how they dress.

Trans Barbadians' contact with the state as migrants or asylum seekers has been treated as suspect rather than protected. The 2011 investigation into gay Barbadians claiming refugee status in Canada, the 2016 statements by Foreign Minister Maxine McClean, and the 2016 report of more than 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States all frame such applications as an abuse risk; UGLAAB said it would investigate the same allegations.
outOfScopeNotes:
Identity-document processes and legal gender recognition for trans Barbadians are not covered by any source assembled here, so the requirements, route and timeframe for changing gender markers on Barbadian documents remain unresolved.

No findings appear on access to transition-related healthcare, mental health or specialist care for trans residents; the only health provisions identified are the Barbados Fertility Centre's IVF and artificial insemination for lesbian couples, the illegal status of surrogacy, and UGLAAB's work on AIDS.

No findings appear on trans-specific custody or parental-rights outcomes. Family-law material reaches only adoption, surrogacy and family recognition, all of which concern same-sex couples as such rather than trans parents.

No findings appear on the treatment of LGBT minors, detention of unaccompanied youth, or school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education. The only youth-adjacent legal detail is that under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, 'serious indecency' carried a maximum penalty of ten years where the act was committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older.

The current status of sections 9 and 12 of the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154) after the December 2022 decriminalisation, and the outcome of the Inter-American Commission petition filed in 2018, are not resolved in these sources. Whether any screening, declaration or health requirement applies specifically to trans entrants at Barbadian border control is likewise not sourced here.
